action.new:
Reading the :attr:`port` attribute will raise a :exc:`ValueError` if
   an invalid port is specified in the URL.  See section
   :ref:`urlparse-result-object` for more information on the result object.

   The :attr:`port` attribute is validated only when it is accessed, not
   when the URL is parsed.  Both :func:`urlsplit` and :func:`urlparse`
   construct the result object successfully; a :exc:`ValueError` is raised
   only when :attr:`port` is accessed and the port component in the URL is
   invalid.  A valid port is a string of ASCII decimal digits representing
   an integer in the range 0 to 65535 inclusive; an empty or absent port
   yields :const:`None`.

   .. doctest::
      :options: +NORMALIZE_WHITESPACE

      >>> from urllib.parse import urlsplit
      >>> p = urlsplit("http://example.com:80/")
      >>> p.port
      80
      >>> p = urlsplit("http://example.com:0/")
      >>> p.port
      0
      >>> p = urlsplit("http://example.com:65535/")
      >>> p.port
      65535
      >>> p = urlsplit("http://example.com/")
      >>> p.port
      >>> p = urlsplit("http://example.com:/")
      >>> p.port

      A port number outside the range 0-65535, or a port that is not a
      string of ASCII decimal digits, raises :exc:`ValueError` on access:

      >>> p = urlsplit("http://example.com:65536/")
      >>> try:
      ...     p.port
      ... except ValueError as e:
      ...     print(e)
      Port out of range 0-65535
      >>> p = urlsplit("http://example.com:-1/")
      >>> try:
      ...     p.port
      ... except ValueError as e:
      ...     print(e)
      Port could not be cast to integer value as '-1'
      >>> p = urlsplit("http://example.com:abc/")
      >>> try:
      ...     p.port
      ... except ValueError as e:
      ...     print(e)
      Port could not be cast to integer value as 'abc'
